title: National Book Festival: Big Crowds and Big Personalities
content:
-NOTE: Our publication schedule was altered last week to accomodate reporting on the death of Dolly Parton. This piece, scheduled for last week, appears now. We knew you’d understand.

The 2026 National Book Festival arrived in style in late August, drawing tens of thousands of bibliophiles, many of whom turned up in festive shirts emblazoned with mottos such as “reading is my favorite sport,” “unreliable narrator,” “sorry, I’m booked” and “bookmarks are for quitters.”

More than 45,000 people attended this year’s event (Aug. 22) at the D.C. convention center, which showcased more than 80 authors and a pavillion full of programs featuring the Library’s collections and resources.

“The promise of a great library is that it opens doors,” said Acting Librarian of Congress Robert R. Newlen, in a short speech that opened the festival. “The Library of Congress has more doors to open than any other library in the world and we hope that you will walk through many of them. Today we have the extraordinary privilege of bringing together some of the most compelling writers and thinkers of our time with all of you, the people who love their work.”

title: Ann Patchett Accepts Prize for American Fiction, Delights SRO National Book Festival Audience
content:
-NOTE: Our publication schedule was altered last week to accomodate reporting on the death of Dolly Parton. This piece, scheduled for last week, appears now. We knew you’d understand.

Ann Patchett accepted the Library’s 2026 Prize for American Fiction at the  National Book Festival, on stage with friend and fellow author Tayari Jones and in front of a standing-room-only crowd of more than 1,100 adoring fans, but she wasn’t entirely sure she wanted to be there.

“I feel like I’m too young for lifetime achievement,” she said, drawing a huge laugh from the crowd.

Patchett (62, for the record) overcame her tongue-in-cheek concerns that the honor was “the nail in the coffin” and accepted the award from Robert R. Newlen, the acting Librarian of Congress.

She might have been mollified by his description of one of the Library’s highest honors, given annually since 2008.

“The prize honors an American literary writer whose body of work is distinguished not only for its mastery of the art, but also for the originality and thought and imagination,” Newlen said.

title: An (Extremely) Fond Farewell to Dolly Parton, Library Friend and Children’s Literacy Champion
content:
Dolly Parton, the beloved country music legend and pop culture icon who died Tuesday, was also a tireless advocate for children’s literacy whose Imagination Library was given one of Library’s highest honors, part of her long association with the national library.

In the 2021 Library of Congress Literacy Awards, the Imagination Library, an initiative of Parton’s Dollywood Foundation, was awarded the David M. Rubenstein Prize of $150,000 for the program’s phenomenal national and international success.

“Dolly Parton’s work was precisely what we envisioned this prize rewarding,” Rubenstein said. “A well-run, highly dedicated literacy program that operated both with passion and a clear sense of mission. It was a privilege to know her and her work.”

The program started in Parton’s home county in rural east Tennessee in 1995 with 1,760 children under age 5 enrolled. Each child received one free book mailed to their home monthly for up to 60 months; therefore each child would have their own library when they started first grade.
